newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU homes in on pact for new treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU homes in on pact for new treaty.

text.p: A new European Union treaty is beginning to take shape with many believing that it can be agreed in June if the Labour Party wins the British election.
Diplomats say that contrary to earlier expectations, it may now be possible for the 15 nations to sign a pact at the Amsterdam EU summit on June 16 and 17.
"The outline of a final deal is now visible, said one EU diplomat.
Disagreements over a broad swathe of issues had previously led most in the EU to say privately that the negotiations would drag on past the summit.
But a combination of lower expectations, creative negotiating and the prospect of a new, more EU-friendly British government has changed things.

Britain's Conservative government, which staunchly defends national sovereignty, has been viewed as a major hurdle to reaching a decision. But the Labour Party, seen as much more flexible, is expected to win a May 1 election.

The Dutch EU presidency on Friday unveiled an updated version of the draft treaty to be presented to EU foreign ministers on Tuesday when they meet in Italy's capital to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome.
Although a number of controversial issues are contained in the draft treaty, most EU officials believe it has the contours of what will eventually be agreed. These include:
-- Creating an area of security and free circulation five years after agreement on a new treaty. Britain and Ireland would be given some form of opt-out from a plan to lift all border checks.

-- Giving slightly more responsibility to the European Parliament, limiting the number of members of the European Commission, moving modestly towards more majority voting and giving larger countries more say in decision making.
-- Adopting treaty language on employment and the environment.
-- Strengthening cooperation in foreign policy matters by creating a planning unit and having EU leaders define the bloc's policies in certain, specified areas.

One key area of disagreement, however, is expected to be aired at the Treaty of Rome celebrations when France and Germany push for the incorporation of the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping into the EU proper.

Although the two powers are supported by Spain, Luxembourg, Belgium, Italy and the Netherlands, the plan faces intense opposition from Britain and the bloc's neutral countries -- Sweden, Ireland, Finland and Austria.
